html:
The burning of the Mycenaean palace at Pylos, in the southwest of the Peloponnese, around 1180 BCE. Tradition links it with Nestor, the old king of Pylos in Homer's poems.

The fire was part of the Late Bronze Age collapse, when palaces across Mycenaean Greece and the eastern Mediterranean were destroyed. Who set it is unknown.

The fire had one lucky effect. The palace kept its records on unbaked clay tablets, written in the Linear B script, and the blaze baked about a thousand of them hard. Carl Blegen found them when he began digging in 1939. In 1952 Michael Ventris showed the script wrote an early form of Greek. The tablets list workers, sheep, bronze, rowers and offerings to gods such as Zeus and Poseidon, a picture of a palace economy in its final year.
